title: Removing devices and machine tunnels through the API and SDKs

prose.text: Three POST calls remove devices: a soft remove, a force remove, and a machine-tunnel remove. Paths and SDK function names are generated; the states they act on are in [[zcc.devices.lifecycle]].

prose.label: Soft and force remove.
prose.text: What each call does and the criteria it needs: [[zcc.api.devices-wire:soft-remove]], [[zcc.api.devices-wire:force-remove]], [[zcc.api.devices-wire:remove-by-criteria]]. The platform codes for `osType` are in [[zcc.api.conventions:os-type-codes]].

prose.label: Python request body.
prose.text: {{python-remove-os-type}} {{python-remove-example-os-code-raises}} {{python-remove-username-example}} Whether the API accepts `username` for `userName` is open {{gap:username-key-accepted}}.

prose.label: Machine tunnels.
prose.text: A changed machine token does not replace existing machine tunnels: [[zcc.entitlements.zpa:machine-token-change]]. {{machine-tunnel-call}} The Go SDK sends the hostnames differently from the contract [[zcc.api.devices-wire:machine-tunnel-hostnames]]. {{python-machine-tunnel-keys}} What a machine-tunnel removal leaves in place is open {{gap:machine-tunnel-removal-scope}}.

remove-page-size.statement: Both remove calls take a `pageSize` query parameter that defaults to 30; the soft-remove contract gives a maximum of 5000.

go-remove-page-size.statement: The Go `SoftRemoveDevices` and `ForceRemoveDevices` always send `pageSize`: a caller's value of 0 or less becomes 50 and a value over 5000 becomes 5000, so the Go default is 50, not the API's 30.

machine-tunnel-call.statement: The machine-tunnel remove call takes either `hostName` (a comma-separated list) or `machineToken` as query parameters, not both; its contract also defines a body with a `hostNames` array and `machineToken`.

expect.description:
Remove machine tunnel devices.

Note: For the parameters described below, you can specify either hostName or machineToken but not both.
Comma-separated list of hostnames for the device.

python-machine-tunnel-keys.statement: The Python `remove_machine_tunnel` camel-cases both its query parameters and its keyword arguments, so its example's `host_names=[...]` goes in the body as `hostNames`, the contract's body key. Its docstring's Args instead document a `hostnames` keyword and a `query_params.hostname` key; neither has an underscore, so both go out unchanged as `hostnames` and `hostname`, matching neither the contract's `hostNames` body key nor its `hostName` query key.
python-machine-tunnel-keys.conditions: Extended per verifier with the docstring's Args keys, traced through the SDK's camel-casing of keyword arguments and (non-ZPA) query parameters.

username-key-accepted.title: Whether the remove calls accept `username` in place of `userName`
username-key-accepted.detail: The contract's body key is `userName`; a Python caller following the `remove_devices` example sends `username`. Whether the server matches it, ignores it, or rejects the call for lacking a criterion is not shown.
username-key-accepted.blocks: removing a user's devices through the Python SDK as documented

machine-tunnel-removal-scope.title: What removing a machine tunnel leaves on the device record
machine-tunnel-removal-scope.detail: Unverified legacy statement: removing the machine tunnel removes only the machine-tunnel component of a device record, leaving the user tunnel and the Client Connector install intact, and is used to clean up stale or conflicting machine-tunnel registrations without deregistering the device.
machine-tunnel-removal-scope.blocks: deciding between a machine-tunnel removal and a device removal
